name: Ja'fer Chelebi
bio: Ja'fer Chelebi, known as Taji-zade, was the elder son of Taji Bey, a counsellor of Prince Bayezid at Amasiya. He studied under the leading scholars of the day, taught at the College of Mahmud Pasha in Constantinople, and, under Sultan Bayezid II, became Nishanji (Chancellor of the Divan), the first holder of that office to be given the rank of Pasha. Under Selim I he served as Qazi-Asker of Anatolia, and in August 1514 (Rejeb 920 A.H.), accused of inciting the janissaries to revolt, he was beheaded; Gibb, who gives no year of birth, records that Selim afterwards regretted the act.

He left a Diwan, the mesnevi Heves-Name or Book of Love-Desire (said to have been written about 1493-4 after a love affair with the wife of a scholar), and, according to one biographer, a facetious poem. Gibb finds his lyrics elegant and learned but lacking passion, and notes that he used his own name in place of a pen-name. The poems here are Gibb's English verse translations from A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902), chapter X; dates and biographical details follow Gibb.

poems.title: From the Spring Qasida
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.note: Gibb's no. 133. A few couplets from the Spring Qasida; the last couplet is from its panegyric.
poems.text:
Lo the radiant beauty-tulip dons her shift of rosy hue,
And with silver studs adorn it bright and sheen the drops of dew.

Now the thorn hath bared his lancet for to bleed the rose's branch;
Now the gold-cap narcisse maketh ready stool and basin too.

Look, 'twould seem the breeze hath ruffled there the flowing streamlet's heart;
For that all its face is knitted, and that naught but frowns we view.

Seeing how a jewelled besom is becoming for thy court
Hangs the perspiration 'Aden pearls the beauties' tresses to.

poems.title: From the Hunt Qasida
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.note: Gibb's no. 134. A few lines from the Hunt Qasida; the last couplet is from its panegyric.
poems.text:
Whensoe'er in winter's season doth the King of happy sway
Make with blood of beasts a tulip-garth of mount and desert-way,

Ranged in ranks upon the deer the heart-empiercing arrows stand;
'Lo, the loved one's eye adorned with the lashes' shafts', thou'dst say.

Since by kissing of thy hand his foot hath honoured been, O King,
Leaveth not the hawk to kiss his talons ever night or day.

poems.title: Ghazel (Fondly do I love a witching charmer dear)
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
Fondly do I love a witching charmer dear, I'll say not who;
Though I yield my life a-yearning after her, I'll say not who.

Though the soul win not its goal, without her knows the heart no rest,
Her my spirit's rest, and her my heart's repair, I'll say not who.

Though that many a sore for dolour burns my heart on tulip wise,
Who she is, yon mole-besprinkled Sovran fair, I'll say not who.

Though that they should cleave my body slit on slit e'en like the comb,
I shall name her not whose tresses are my snare, I'll say not who.

Ja'fer, though they cut me piecemeal, all to fragments like my ear,
Who she is, yon ear-ringed lovesome charmer dear, I'll say not who.

poems.title: Ghazel (Whensoe'er I think to tell my dear mine anguish and dismay)
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)

poems.title: Ghazel (Since that the bud to ape thy lip did dare)
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
Since that the bud to ape thy lip did dare,
Its mouth in anger do the breezes tear.

Through passion for that cypress-form of thine
The pine-tree maddened seeks the mountain bare.

They say who see the down upon thy cheek,
'A violet growing on a rose-leaf fair!'

Those basil lines about thy lip the judge
Before the lines of Yaqut doth prefer.

Above his grave will rose and tulip grow,
If Ja'fer die, thy cheek desiring e'er.

poems.title: Ghazel (Fill the golden goblet, skinker, fill, the wine unmingled pour)
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
Fill the golden goblet, skinker, fill, the wine unmingled pour!
Let the hypocrite bedrench his yellow face with tears of gore.

Let the fairy-beauties glow impassioned, let them rend their shifts!
At the banquet be there opened into Heaven many a door!

O'er thine eyebrows make those ruffled locks of thine to dangle fair;
For the cross's place is aye the paynim mihrab from of yore.

Cypress fair, without thee unto me as eddy-whirls of blood
Show the fresh and tender tulips growing by the river-shore.

Those are many souls demented, worn to hairs for passion's stress;
Hair they are not, Ja'fer, yonder ambered locks, I tell thee sure.

poems.title: Ghazel (Would that I had been nor servitor, nay, neither served e'er)
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.text:
Would that I had been nor servitor, nay, neither served e'er!
Would that I had bode unbeing, to the world had journeyed ne'er!

Since my dust found being, and I might nor gold nor silver be,
Would that I had bode a clod or stone or handful pebbles there!

But since grow I must, and reckoned 'mongst the blossoms might not be,
Would that I had bode a leek or onion for which none doth care!

When I rose to life, O would I had remained amongst the brutes;
Since I might not be a bulbul, then an owl or crow, I swear!

Since at last I must be man, and subtlety of soul not mine,
Would that I had been a dullard callous-natured, void of care!

For that then, O Lord, at least I had not suffered these desires;
Would that I had had not any lot in Love nor any share!

Since that death to me were better than to live with all this woe,
Would, O Ja'fer, that a dead man, struck from off the roll, I were!

poems.title: From the Heves-Nama
poems.author: Ja'fer Chelebi
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. II (1902)
poems.note: Gibb's no. 140. Verses from the introduction to the Heves-Nama (the Book of Love-Desire).
poems.text:
In Turkish 'tis these two who famous shine:
Sheykhî and Ahmed, O dear friend of mine.
Though Sheykhî, in good sooth, 'fore God on high,
Hath skill of speech, as no one may deny,
Of purity of language naught he knows,
And many an uncouth word his poem shows.
And though in Ahmed Pasha there is grace,
And purity finds in his speech a place,
Yet is he nothing skilled in eloquence,
Nor can he bind his words with elegance;
His words have beauty, but no charm they bear,
Like paintings in a church, no life is there.
